clue.text: Those setting up before Oval boundaries dispatched in the capital

indicators.note: before places the first piece ahead of the second in the answer
in a down clue, setting something up means writing its letters from the bottom upwards

parts.note: the people setting this puzzle are 'us', the setters speaking of themselves

indicators.note: the boundaries of the word Oval are its outer letters, and dispatching them leaves only the inside

explanation.surface: Groundsmen preparing the Oval, a London cricket ground, before a match, with the capital as backdrop.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Those setting' are the setters, US, which 'up' turns to SU in a down light. 'Boundaries dispatched' strips the O and L from Oval to leave VA. The Oval is a London cricket ground.
explanation.definitionFit: Suva is the capital city of Fiji, so 'the capital' works as a general clue to it.

clue.text: Admirer of one-day international on the up? Dead right

indicators.note: in a down light, 'on the up' means the letters climb, so the abbreviation is read from bottom to top

parts.note: ODI is the standard abbreviation for a one-day international cricket match
late means dead, as in 'the late king'

explanation.surface: A fan of one-day cricket asks if they're on the rise and gets a hearty 'Dead right'.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On the up' reverses the abbreviation in this down light. 'Dead right' looks like an exclamation of agreement but splits into two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who worships idols, or more loosely an adoring devotee, is an admirer.

clue.text: E.g. single run scored with square cut, possibly

parts.note: R is the cricket scorer's abbreviation for a run

indicators.note: possibly says the remaining letters might be arranged some other way
cut means a letter is removed from the word scored

parts.note: S stands for square here, as the setter uses it

explanation.surface: A batsman notches a single run with a square cut, a cricket stroke played sideways off the back foot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Square cut' is a real cricket shot, but here 'square' gives S, which 'cut' removes; 'possibly' rearranges the remaining CORED after R.
explanation.definitionFit: A single is one kind of record released by a band, so it is an example of the wider category.

clue.text: One making you go to see English XI at Oval, when not initially bothered

indicators.note: bothered means disturbed or stirred up, so these letters are thrown into a new order

parts.note: an eleven, the cricket team, written in Roman numerals

indicators.note: says the word Oval loses its first letter

explanation.surface: A fan off to watch the England eleven at the Oval, a London cricket ground, finally keen enough to bother.
explanation.walkthrough: 'When not initially' trims Oval to VAL; 'bothered' rearranges XI, AT and VAL into LAXATIV, with E for 'English' added. 'To see' only links.
explanation.definitionFit: A laxative is a medicine that makes you go to the toilet, a euphemistic description.

clue.text: People heading off to the middle to play again

indicators.note: says the word for people loses its first letter, its head

parts.note: men means people, a group of persons
the core of something is its middle

explanation.surface: Batsmen walk out to the middle of the pitch to resume play.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The middle' sounds like the cricket square, but it gives CORE.
explanation.definitionFit: An extra performance demanded by the audience is the band or player performing again.

clue.text: Present time in Yorkshire, duck

parts.note: now means the present moment

explanation.surface: Someone in Yorkshire presented with a duck as a gift at this time.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a duck is a score of zero. Yorkshire is a northern English county whose dialect uses this word for nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: The northern dialect word means nothing, and in cricket a duck is a score of nothing.

clue.text: See 16
Relative getting amongst the runs (a lot) in county town

indicators.note: getting amongst means one word is placed inside the other

parts.note: a ton is a hundred runs in cricket, which is a lot
an aunt is a relative

explanation.surface: A family member scores a century at a county ground.
explanation.walkthrough: TAUNTON is the county town of Somerset, in south-west England, and home of Somerset County Cricket Club.
explanation.definitionFit: Taunton is the administrative centre of the English county of Somerset.

clue.text: Walk-on part in Test is observed uninterrupted

definitions.meaning: the part of the foot one walks on, below the toes
'Test is' with no break between the words reads as testis, a slang equivalent of which is this word

explanation.surface: A bit-part player in a Test match watched without a break.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Walk-on part' suggests a minor acting role but means part of the foot; 'Test is' closed up gives TESTIS. A Test is an international cricket match.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses are slang or anatomical: the padded part of the sole, and an informal word for a testicle.

clue.text: Batsman having got amongst the bowlers this amount?

definitions.text: Batsman having got amongst the bowlers

parts.note: the answer read as instructions says the letters of MAN OUT, oddly arranged, produce the word amount

explanation.surface: A batsman stranded among the fielding side, asking how many he has scored.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as wordplay, the answer is ODD (an anagram signal) acting on MAN OUT, whose letters rearrange to AMOUNT.
explanation.definitionFit: A lone batsman among a team of bowlers is the one who does not fit in, the misfit.

clue.text: Tired, having run 3 as opener? Shame!

indicators.note: as opener says this piece starts the answer

parts.note: refers to the answer at 3-down, whose synonym is disc, a vinyl recording

indicators.note: run is used in the sense of melted or mixed, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A weary batsman who opened the innings and ran three: what a disgrace!
explanation.walkthrough: '3' is not a number of runs but a cross-reference to 3-down, which gives DISC; 'having run' rearranges TIRED to REDIT.
explanation.definitionFit: To bring shame upon someone is to damage their reputation, so the noun and verb senses match.

clue.text: Saw old man keeping note of the score

indicators.note: keeping means holding something inside

parts.note: old man is slang for father, dad
te is a note of the sol-fa scale, found in a musical score

explanation.surface: Someone spotted a father keeping a note of the cricket score.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Score' suggests runs on the board but means a musical score, giving the note TE.
explanation.definitionFit: To be seeing someone is to go out with them romantically, so 'saw' matches the past tense.

clue.text: Hit strongly in front of wicket around end of second over

definitions.text: Hit strongly in front of wicket

indicators.note: end of means the final letter of the word second
around means the letters are turned about into a new order

explanation.surface: A batsman drives powerfully at the end of the second over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'End of' gives D from 'second', and 'around' rearranges D and OVER. In cricket an over is six balls.
explanation.definitionFit: A drive is a powerful cricket shot played straight in front of the wicket, so the past tense fits.

clue.text: Good shots through cover from those cutting half-heartedly

indicators.note: the heart of the word for cutters is a double letter, and half of it is dropped

parts.note: snippers are people or tools that snip, cut

explanation.surface: A batsman plays fine cover drives, praised by fielders who cut half-hearted figures.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cover' suggests the cricket fielding position but means shelter; the middle PP of SNIPPERS loses one P.
explanation.definitionFit: Marksmen who fire from a hidden position are skilled shooters working through cover.

clue.text: Square cut regularly ends in boundaries

indicators.note: in places the picked letters inside the boundaries

parts.note: in cricket the two boundary scores are six and ...

indicators.note: ends picks the last letter of each of the two words

explanation.surface: A square cut, a sideways cricket stroke, regularly ends in boundaries.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Square cut' reads as the cricket shot, but 'Square' alone is the definition; 'ends' and 'in' do the rest. A six and a four are the two boundary scores in cricket.
explanation.definitionFit: Eight multiplied by itself makes this number, so it is a perfect square.

clue.text: See 14
A number of centuries from County Cricket Club openers

definitions.meaning: ... centuries in cricket, a ... runs each, total this number
the opening letters of these ... words are CCC, which in Roman numerals is this number

explanation.surface: A county club whose opening batsmen score a string of centuries.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Openers' suggests opening batsmen, but means the initials CCC, read as Roman numerals.
explanation.definitionFit: Each century is a hundred, so three of them make the total; CCC is Roman notation for it.

clue.text: Running flat out, and initially excessively

indicators.note: running is used in the sense of loose or flowing, so the letters are rearranged
initially picks the first letter of the word and

explanation.surface: A batsman sprints flat out between the wickets, overdoing it from the start.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Running' rearranges FLAT OUT plus A, the first letter of 'and'.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to an excessive degree, as in 'generous to a fault'.

clue.text: Sly fellow with neat playing, essentially

parts.note: neat is an old word for cattle, so an ox

indicators.note: essentially picks the central letter, the essence, of the word playing

explanation.surface: A cunning fellow who plays a neat, tidy game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Neat' looks like 'tidy' but is the archaic word for cattle, giving OX.
explanation.definitionFit: Being crafty or cunning like a fox is being sly.

clue.text: Was last man dismissed for sex act?

parts.note: a batsman who is out is said to have fallen, so fell
the last man out falls at the tenth wicket, 'at 10', with the figures 1 and 0 written as the letters I and O

explanation.surface: Was the last batsman sent off for indecency?
explanation.walkthrough: The last man dismissed fell at 10, the tenth wicket; reading 10 as IO gives the answer. 'Was' and 'for' link.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin-derived term names oral stimulation of the penis, a sexual practice.

clue.text: It's no good wearing a South African jumper in this country

indicators.note: wearing means one piece is put inside another, as clothing goes on

parts.note: an eland is a large African antelope, a leaping animal; 'jumper' plays on the sweater sense

explanation.surface: A complaint that a South African sweater is useless in this country's climate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jumper' is British for a sweater, but here means a leaping antelope; 'wearing' puts the abbreviation inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: The paper is English, so 'this country' is the home nation of the setter and readers.

clue.text: Playing at Oval for a bit of radio commentary cake

indicators.note: radio commentary is spoken aloud, so the hidden letters are heard rather than read
a bit of says the letters needed are part of a longer stretch of words

parts.note: the letters run across the end of playing, all of at and the start of Oval

explanation.surface: Cricket on radio at the Oval, a London cricket ground, where commentators are famously sent cakes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A bit of' takes GATO from 'playinG AT Oval'; 'radio commentary' says that is spoken, and GATO sounds like the French-derived word.
explanation.definitionFit: A rich layered sponge cake is known by this French name.

clue.text: Attractive girl makes an easy catch

definitions.meaning: a ... bird is dated slang for a pretty young woman
in cricket a ... is a gentle, simple catch for a fielder

explanation.surface: A pretty girl is an easy conquest.
explanation.definitionFit: One word covers both senses: dated slang for a pretty woman and cricket slang for a simple catch.

clue.text: Some made centuries, honest!

indicators.note: Some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A batsman insists they really did score centuries, honestly.
explanation.definitionFit: A decent person is fair and upright, which is what being honest means.

clue.text: Surprisingly catch it, stopping a run or 4?

definitions.note: refers to the answer at 4-down, a purgative

indicators.note: stopping means the pieces are plugged into the middle of the jumble
surprisingly suggests the letters of catch it come out in an unexpected order

parts.note: R is the cricket abbreviation for a run

explanation.surface: A fielder unexpectedly catches it, preventing a single or a boundary four.
explanation.walkthrough: '4' looks like a boundary but is a cross-reference to 4-down. 'Surprisingly' rearranges CATCH IT to CATHTIC, and 'stopping' puts A and R inside.
explanation.definitionFit: A cathartic is a purgative medicine, which is what 4-down describes.

clue.text: Readies cricketers as summer holiday starts

indicators.note: starts picks the first letter of each of the four words

explanation.surface: Cricketers get themselves ready as the summer holiday begins.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Readies' looks like a verb but is British slang for ready money.
explanation.definitionFit: The readies is informal British slang for money in hand, notes and coins.

clue.text: A group of players featuring in Oval's offering too

parts.note: the LSO, London Symphony Orchestra, is a group of musical players; the run in 'Oval's offering' is no coincidence but the setter's second route

explanation.surface: A team of players appears in what the Oval, a London cricket ground, has on offer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Players' suggests cricketers but means musicians. The clue has a second way in: 'featuring in' also points to the answer sitting inside 'OvAL'S Offering'.
explanation.definitionFit: Also and too are synonyms, both meaning in addition.

clue.text: Ultimately running in wrong for three balls?

indicators.note: in places the letter inside the other word

parts.note: a sin is a wrong

indicators.note: ultimately picks the final letter of running

explanation.surface: A batsman runs wrongly after three deliveries.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Three balls' suggests deliveries in cricket, but means the pawnbroker's sign of three golden balls.
explanation.definitionFit: Three hanging golden balls are the traditional emblem displayed outside a pawnbroker's shop.

clue.text: Attack a spinner beginning to get turn in middle of season

indicators.note: beginning picks the first letter of spinner
in middle of places the turn inside the seasoning word

parts.note: to season food is to salt it
a U-turn is a turn, so U

explanation.surface: A spin bowler is brought on to attack midway through the season.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Season' looks like the cricket calendar but is the verb, giving SALT.
explanation.definitionFit: An assault is a violent attack, so the two words are synonyms.

clue.text: Losing wife (or wicket!) spoils one's life

indicators.note: losing says a letter is taken away

parts.note: spoils are the gains or winnings taken
W is the abbreviation for wife, and also for wicket in cricket scoring

explanation.surface: A gambler who loses his wife, or a batsman his wicket, finds their winnings ruined.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spoils' looks like a verb but is the noun, plunder or gains.
explanation.definitionFit: A long life is called a good innings, the cricket term for a batsman's spell at the crease.
